objectives: Two new relative pairs: B major with G♯ minor, and D♭ major with B♭ minor
B major has five sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯); D♭ major has five flats (B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭)
G♯ minor completes the sharp minor keys and B♭ minor the flat minor keys at this grade

concept.title: Grade 4 keys
concept.body: Two more major keys arrive, each with five accidentals, and each brings its relative minor. B major has five sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯) and pairs with G♯ minor; D♭ major has five flats (B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭) and pairs with B♭ minor. The relative minor's tonic still sits a minor 3rd below its major partner — count down from B to G♯, and from D♭ to B♭.

teach.smartTip: Count three semitones — a minor 3rd — down from the major tonic to find the relative minor: B down to G♯, D♭ down to B♭.
teach.didYouKnow: B major and D♭ major sit a semitone apart on the piano, and B is the same key as C♭ — yet their key signatures are opposites: five sharps versus five flats.

objectives: Name a major key by counting the sharps or flats in its signature
B major has five sharps; D♭ major has five flats
Five is one more than the four you met at Grade 3 — the count is the whole difference

concept.title: Counting to five
concept.body: Grade 3 took you to four accidentals: E major with four sharps, A♭ major with four flats. Grade 4 adds one more of each. B major has five sharps; D♭ major has five flats. Telling sharps from flats is only half the job — you have to count them exactly, because a single accidental is the whole difference between B major and E major, or between D♭ major and A♭ major. The order never varies, so the fifth symbol is always the one that tells you which of the pair you are looking at.

teach.smartTip: Count first, then decide: five sharps is B major, four is E major; five flats is D♭ major, four is A♭ major.
teach.didYouKnow: The order the sharps appear in is always the same — F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯ — so B major's fifth sharp is A♯, and reading that last sharp is a quick way to confirm the key.

objectives: Build B major and D♭ major, five sharps and five flats
Five of the seven letters carry an accidental, and two do not
Naming which two are unaltered is faster than checking all seven

concept.title: Five accidentals, and the two that are left alone
concept.body: B major has five sharps and D♭ major five flats. With five of the seven letters altered, it is quicker to remember the exceptions than the rule. In B major the two plain letters are B and E; every other letter is sharpened. In D♭ major the plain letters are F and C; every other letter is flattened. Build the scale the same way as always — the seven letters in order from the keynote, then the accidental each one needs — and use the exceptions as a check at the end rather than as the method.

teach.smartTip: Name the two unaltered letters first: B and E in B major, F and C in D♭ major. Everything else takes the accidental.
teach.didYouKnow: B major and C♭ major are the same sounds written two ways, but C♭ major needs seven flats to B major’s five sharps. Composers pick the spelling that costs fewer accidentals, which is why you meet B major and not C♭ major.

lessons.title: Harmonic and melodic minor in the new keys

objectives: The harmonic and melodic minor rules you know now apply to G♯ minor and B♭ minor
G♯ harmonic minor's raised 7th is F𝄪 (F double-sharp) — the first double-sharp in the course
B♭ harmonic minor's raised 7th is A♮ — raising a flatted 7th can land back on a natural

concept.title: Harmonic and melodic minor in the new keys
concept.body: The same rules apply: harmonic minor raises the natural minor's 7th a semitone; melodic minor raises the 6th and 7th going up and reverts coming down. Spelling the raised 7th on the 7th letter forces a double-sharp in G♯ minor — its natural 7th is F♯, so raising it a semitone gives F double-sharp (F𝄪), written with the 𝄪 sign, never G natural. B♭ minor is gentler: its natural 7th is A♭, so the raised 7th is simply A♮.

teach.smartTip: Always raise on the same letter. G♯ minor's 7th letter is F, so its raised 7th must stay an F — an F♯ raised a semitone is F double-sharp, not G.
teach.didYouKnow: A double-sharp (𝄪) raises a note by two semitones — a whole tone — from its natural pitch, so F𝄪 sounds the same as G, but naming it F keeps every letter of the G♯ minor scale distinct.

objectives: A chromatic scale moves entirely in semitones, using every pitch between its tonic and the octave
That is twelve semitone steps — thirteen notes counting both the tonic and its octave
The usual ascending spelling uses sharps: a sharpened letter fills each whole-tone gap, and none is added where letters are already a semitone apart (E–F, B–C)

concept.title: The chromatic scale
concept.body: A chromatic scale climbs entirely by semitones, touching every note between the tonic and its octave — twelve steps, thirteen notes. Ascending, it is usually written with sharps: between two letters a whole tone apart you insert the lower letter sharpened (C, C♯, D, D♯, E …), and where two letters are already only a semitone apart — E to F, and B to C — you add nothing. The key signature plays no part: a chromatic scale carries no key of its own.

teach.smartTip: Going up, reach for sharps first. Every whole-tone gap gets a sharpened note wedged in; the two natural semitones, E–F and B–C, are left alone.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Chromatic’ comes from the Greek chroma, meaning colour — the extra notes between the scale steps were heard as adding colour to the plain diatonic scale.

objectives: Every degree of a scale has a technical name, not just a number
In order: tonic (1st), supertonic (2nd), mediant (3rd), subdominant (4th), dominant (5th), submediant (6th), leading note (7th)
The tonic and dominant are the two strongest degrees; the leading note sits a semitone below the tonic and pulls up to it

concept.title: Technical names of scale degrees
concept.body: Each note of a scale has a technical name describing its role. Counting up from the tonic: tonic (1st), supertonic (2nd), mediant (3rd), subdominant (4th), dominant (5th), submediant (6th), and leading note (7th). The tonic is home and the dominant — a 5th above — is its strongest relation. ‘Mediant’ sits midway between tonic and dominant; ‘subdominant’ is a 5th below the tonic (the ‘sub’ mirroring the dominant below rather than above), and ‘submediant’ midway between tonic and subdominant going down. The leading note lies a semitone under the tonic and leads the ear back up to it.

teach.smartTip: Anchor on tonic (1) and dominant (5). Subdominant is the 4th — think of it as the dominant measured a 5th *below* the tonic instead of above.
teach.didYouKnow: The leading note earns its name from its pull: sitting just a semitone below the tonic, it sounds unfinished until it steps up to resolve — which is exactly why the harmonic minor raises it.

objectives: The breve is the longest note value at this grade — worth two semibreves, or eight crotchet beats
It is drawn as an open notehead with a short vertical line on each side (or a square notehead)
You meet it in broad, slow passages; it is rare but worth recognising

concept.title: The breve
concept.body: The breve is the longest note value you'll meet — worth two semibreves, or eight crotchet beats. It is drawn as an open (hollow) notehead flanked by a short vertical line on each side, sometimes as a square notehead instead. Because it lasts so long, it only fits bars with room for it — you'll see it in slow, broad music rather than busy passages.

teach.smartTip: A breve is two semibreves joined — eight crotchet beats in all, twice the length of a semibreve.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Breve’ comes from the Latin brevis, ‘short’ — it was once one of the shortest notes in medieval music, before quicker values pushed it all the way to the long end of the scale.

objectives: The breve rest is the longest rest — a silence lasting eight beats, as long as the breve note
It is drawn as a solid block filling the space between the middle two lines of the stave
A breve rest lasts twice as long as a semibreve rest, just as a breve lasts twice a semibreve

concept.title: The longest silence
concept.body: Just as the breve is the longest note, the breve rest is the longest rest — eight crotchet beats, twice the four of a semibreve rest. It sits as a solid block between the middle two lines of the stave, filling the whole space rather than hanging from a line like the semibreve rest. To complete a long bar, count the beats already used and match the gap: a full eight-beat gap calls for the breve rest.

teach.smartTip: Two semibreve rests make a breve rest — eight beats of silence. The block fills the middle space; the semibreve rest only hangs beneath a line.
teach.didYouKnow: The breve rest is so rare that many musicians go years without writing one — it turns up mostly in slow music with very long bars.

objectives: A first dot adds half the note's value; a second dot adds half again — half of the first dot
A double-dotted note therefore lasts one and three-quarter times its plain value
Example: a double-dotted minim = minim + crotchet + quaver = three and a half crotchet beats
A rest takes both dots the same way, and lasts exactly as long as the note it silences

concept.title: Double dots, on notes and on rests
concept.body: A single dot adds half the note's value. A second dot adds half again — but half of the **first** dot, not the note. So a double-dotted note lasts one and three-quarter times its plain value. A double-dotted minim is minim + crotchet + quaver (2 + 1 + ½ = 3½ crotchet beats); a double-dotted crotchet is crotchet + quaver + semiquaver. Each dot is worth half of whatever sits immediately to its left. Rests take dots on the same terms: a double-dotted minim rest is three and a half beats of silence, and a double-dotted crotchet rest is one and three-quarter beats.

teach.smartTip: First dot = half the note; second dot = half the first dot (a quarter of the note). Add them up: 1 + ½ + ¼ = 1¾ of the plain value — for a rest just as for a note.
teach.didYouKnow: Double dots make a dotted rhythm crisper — the following short note becomes even shorter and snappier. Baroque overtures and marches lean on this for their dignified, pointed feel.

objectives: A duplet is two notes played in the time of three of the same value
It belongs to compound time, where the beat normally divides into three
A duplet fills one compound beat (a dotted crotchet) with two equal notes instead of three

concept.title: Duplets
concept.body: In compound time the beat divides into three. A duplet borrows one beat for **two** equal notes instead — two played in the time of three. It is written with a bracket and a small ‘2’ over the group. So in 6/8, a duplet fills one dotted-crotchet beat with two notes where three quavers would normally go. It is the mirror image of the triplet you'd meet in simple time.

teach.smartTip: A duplet is a triplet turned inside out: two-in-the-time-of-three in compound time, where a triplet is three-in-the-time-of-two in simple time.
teach.didYouKnow: A duplet lets a composer slip a momentary ‘simple-time’ feel into a compound-time bar — two even beats where the metre expects a lilting three — without changing the time signature.

objectives: The top number decides the family; the bottom number names the note being counted
6, 9 and 12 on top mean compound time — group the beats in threes
The bottom number never decides simple versus compound: 6/4, 6/8 and 6/16 are all compound duple
The minim can be the beat too: 2/2, 3/2 and 4/2 are simple duple, triple and quadruple

concept.title: Reading any time signature
concept.body: To classify a time signature, read the top number first. 2, 3 or 4 means simple time — that many beats, each dividing into two. 6, 9 or 12 means compound time — group the beats in threes, so 6/8 is **two** dotted-crotchet beats, not six. The bottom number only says which note is being counted: 8 the quaver, 4 the crotchet, 16 the semiquaver. In simple time that note is the beat; in compound time three of them make one dotted beat, so 6/16 is two dotted-quaver beats and 6/4 two dotted-minim beats. It never changes simple versus compound — 6/4, 6/8 and 6/16 are all compound duple, just written in bigger or smaller note values. The same reading works when the minim is the beat. 2/2, 3/2 and 4/2 put two, three and four minim beats in a bar, so they are simple duple, triple and quadruple — the family is decided by the top number here exactly as it is everywhere else.

teach.smartTip: Top number first: 2/3/4 is simple, 6/9/12 is compound (divide by three for the beat count). The bottom number is only which note is counted — in compound time it takes three of them to make a beat.
teach.didYouKnow: Fast movements are sometimes written in 6/16 so the page looks less crowded, while slow, broad music may use 6/4 — but both are still a lilting compound duple, exactly like 6/8.

objectives: The rule never changes: one beamed group per beat
In 2/8 and 4/8 the quaver is the beat, so semiquavers beam in pairs
In the /4 and /16 compound metres the beat is a dotted note, so the group is three of the division

concept.title: One rule, any denominator
concept.body: Grade 4 opens metres with quaver and minim beats, and the grouping rule survives all of them unchanged: one beamed group per beat. In 2/8 and 4/8 the beat is a quaver, so semiquavers beam in pairs and each pair is a beat. In 6/4 the beat is a dotted minim, three crotchets long, so a bar of quavers beams as two groups of six. The groups get longer or shorter, but a reader still counts beats by counting beams. Work out the beat from the time signature, then beam that much and break. The bottom number changes which value is written, never the rule. In 9/4 and 12/4 the beat is a dotted minim, so quavers beam in sixes; in 6/16, 9/16 and 12/16 the beat is a dotted quaver, so semiquavers beam in threes. In 4/2 the beat is a minim, and quavers beam in fours.

teach.smartTip: Find the beat, then beam exactly one beat at a time. The denominator alone never tells you.
teach.didYouKnow: 6/4 was standard in Renaissance dance music and came back through Holst and Stravinsky, who liked its long, slow-turning beat.

objectives: Name the interval between **any** two notes now, not only above the tonic
A perfect or major interval made a semitone wider is augmented; a perfect or minor interval made a semitone narrower is diminished
The augmented 4th (e.g. F up to B) and diminished 5th (B up to F) are the classic examples — both span six semitones
Read the key signature before you count: it may sharpen or flatten one of the two notes and change the quality

concept.title: Augmented and diminished intervals
concept.body: Two new qualities join perfect, major and minor. Widen a perfect or major interval by a semitone and it becomes *augmented*; narrow a perfect or minor interval by a semitone and it becomes *diminished*. Find the number first by counting letter names (F–G–A–B is a 4th), then the quality by the semitones. The most common examples are the augmented 4th (F up to B, six semitones) and the diminished 5th (B up to F, also six semitones) — the same distance on the keyboard, named differently by how the notes are spelled. You can now name intervals between any two notes, not just from the key's tonic. The interval may sit in any key set for this grade, so read the key signature first. The same pair of letters can be two different intervals: F up to A is a major 3rd in C major, but in D major the signature sharpens the F, and F♯ up to A is a minor 3rd.

teach.smartTip: Key signature first, then number (count letter names), then quality (count semitones). Bigger than perfect or major is augmented; smaller than perfect or minor is diminished.
teach.didYouKnow: The augmented 4th and diminished 5th — the ‘tritone’ — was once nicknamed diabolus in musica, ‘the devil in music’, for its restless sound that seems to demand resolution.

objectives: The alto (C) clef is a third clef, alongside treble and bass
Its middle line is middle C (C4) — everything else is read from there
It is the viola's everyday clef, keeping that instrument's music on the stave

concept.title: The alto clef
concept.body: The alto clef — also called the C clef — centres on middle C: its middle line IS middle C (C4). It is the viola's everyday clef, keeping that instrument's music on the stave without a forest of ledger lines. Read it like any clef: find middle C on the centre line, then count lines and spaces up or down. The bottom line is F3 and the top line is G4.

teach.smartTip: The two curved arms of the alto clef point straight at the middle line — and that line is middle C. Count every other note from there.
teach.didYouKnow: The alto clef is a movable ‘C clef’: the same symbol shifted up one line becomes the tenor clef (for high cello and bassoon). Sitting on the middle line, it is the alto clef the viola reads.

lessons.title: The alto clef in a key signature

objectives: Name a note in the alto clef when a key signature is printed
A sharp or flat in the signature alters every note of that letter, in every octave
Find the letter first, then apply the signature — the count from middle C never changes

concept.title: Letter first, signature second
concept.body:
Everything you learned about counting from middle C on the middle line still holds. A key signature does not move a single note; it decides what the letters you count to actually sound.

So read in two steps. Step one: count lines and spaces from middle C and get the letter. Step two: look back at the signature and ask whether that letter carries a sharp or a flat. If it does, the note is sharp or flat — in every octave, not only the one the signature prints.

The signature itself is printed at the alto clef's own positions. An F sharp sits on the alto clef's F line, which is the bottom line, not where your eye expects it from the treble. That is the one thing that catches people out, and reading the letter first makes it harmless.

teach.smartTip: Count to the letter, then check the signature. Doing it the other way round is how a note ends up sharp in the wrong octave.
teach.didYouKnow: A viola part in five sharps looks alarming and is not. The player still reads the same nine lines and spaces; the signature simply tells the left hand where to sit.

lessons.title: Octave transposition to and from the alto clef

objectives: Rewrite a melody an octave higher or lower, moving between clefs so it stays on the stave
Every letter name stays the same — only the octave (and the clef) changes
The clef is chosen to keep the transposed melody on the stave, not to decide its direction

concept.title: Octave transposition to and from the alto clef
concept.body: Octave transposition rewrites a melody an octave away while keeping every letter name the same — only the octave changes. The question gives the direction; a different clef is what lets the rewritten melody stay comfortably on the stave: a melody in the alto clef can be written an octave higher in the treble, or an octave lower in the bass. The notes look different on the page, but they are the same letters, just an octave apart.

teach.smartTip: Same letters, new octave. Read the direction from the question, then pick the clef that keeps the result on the stave: alto → treble going up, alto → bass going down.
teach.didYouKnow: Rewriting the same music in another clef and octave is how a viola line might be shared with a violinist or cellist — the clef and octave move, but the tune stays unmistakably the same.

lessons.title: The same pitch in different clefs

objectives: One sounding pitch is written at a different line or space in each clef
Middle C sits below the treble stave, above the bass stave, and on the middle line of the alto clef — three positions, one note
To rewrite a note in another clef, keep the pitch exactly and find where it lives on the new stave

concept.title: One pitch, three staves
concept.body: A clef fixes which pitch each line and space stands for, so the **same** sounding note lands in a different place depending on the clef. Middle C is the clearest case: it hangs on a ledger line just below the treble stave, on a ledger line just above the bass stave, and squarely on the middle line of the alto clef — one pitch, three positions. Rewriting a melody from one clef to another does not change a single sound; you keep every pitch and rhythm exactly, and only re-read where each note sits on the new stave.

teach.smartTip: The note does not move — you do. Keep the exact pitch and ask “where does this sound live on the new clef?”
teach.didYouKnow: This is why an orchestral score stacks different clefs: a cellist reading bass clef and a violist reading alto clef can play the very same note, each written where it sits most cleanly on their own stave.

lessons.title: Primary triads: I, IV and V

objectives: The three primary triads — I, IV and V — are built on the 1st, 4th and 5th degrees of a major scale
In a major key all three are major triads: a root, the note a 3rd above it, and the note a 5th above
Every chord here is in root position, so its lowest note is its root: tonic → I, subdominant → IV, dominant → V

concept.title: Primary triads: I, IV and V
concept.body: A triad is a three-note chord: a root, the note a 3rd above it, and the note a 5th above. The three *primary* triads are built on the most important degrees of the scale — I on the tonic (1st), IV on the subdominant (4th), and V on the dominant (5th). In a major key all three are major triads. Every chord at this grade is in root position, so its lowest note is its root. To name a chord you see, find that lowest note and work out which scale degree it lands on in the given key: root on the tonic is I, on the subdominant IV, on the dominant V. In C major that makes I = C–E–G, IV = F–A–C, and V = G–B–D.

teach.smartTip: Read the key signature, then look at the chord's lowest note — in root position that is the root. If it is the key's 1st degree the chord is I, the 4th degree IV, the 5th degree V.
teach.didYouKnow: I, IV and V are called the primary triads because between them they use every note of the major scale — which is why so much music can be harmonised with just these three chords.

lessons.title: Primary chords in a minor key

objectives: I, IV and V are built on the same three degrees in a minor key
I and IV come out minor; V comes out major, because of the raised 7th
The sharp or natural that raises the 7th is written on the note, never in the key signature

concept.title: Two minor, one major
concept.body: The primary triads sit on the same degrees in a minor key as in a major one: I on the keynote, IV on the 4th, V on the 5th. What changes is how they sound. Build them from the key signature alone and I and IV come out minor, which is what you would expect. V does not. Its middle note is the 7th degree of the scale, and a minor key raises that 7th — the harmonic form — so V comes out major. That is the whole reason V can lead back to the keynote: the raised 7th is a semitone below it and pulls. In A minor the raised 7th is G♯, so V is E, G♯, B rather than E, G, B. The accidental is written against the note, because the key signature spells the natural form.

teach.smartTip: Check the middle note of V. If it carries an accidental the key signature did not give it, that is the raised 7th, and the chord is major.
teach.didYouKnow: This is why so much minor-key music has one stray accidental appearing again and again. It is almost always the raised 7th, arriving with the dominant chord.

objectives: Ornaments are small signs that decorate a note with extra, quicker notes
Six to recognise: trill, turn, upper mordent, lower mordent, acciaccatura, appoggiatura
A trill shakes rapidly with the note above; a mordent flicks once; a turn curls around the note; grace notes (acciaccatura, appoggiatura) are tiny notes printed before the main one

concept.title: Ornaments
concept.body: Ornaments decorate a note with extra, faster notes, written as small signs. A *trill* (tr) shakes rapidly between the written note and the one above it. A *turn* curls around the note — the note above, the note, the note below, and back. An *upper mordent* flicks quickly up to the note above and back; a *lower mordent* flicks down to the note below and back. Two are grace notes, printed small just before the main note: an *acciaccatura* (with a slash through its stem) is crushed in as fast as possible, while an *appoggiatura* (no slash) leans on the beat and borrows time from the main note.

teach.smartTip: A mordent flicks once (up = upper, down = lower); a turn curls both ways around the note; a trill shakes on and on. The two grace notes sit before the main note — the slashed acciaccatura is the quicker.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Acciaccatura’ comes from the Italian acciaccare, ‘to crush’ — it is crushed against the main note so fast the two almost sound at once, then instantly released.

objectives: The orchestra is grouped into four families: strings, woodwind, brass, and percussion
What puts an instrument in its family is how it makes its sound, not where it sits
Every instrument named here belongs to one of the four, and you can place any of them

concept.title: The four families
concept.body: Orchestral instruments fall into four families, and what decides the family is how the sound starts. *Strings* (violin, viola, cello, double bass) are bowed or plucked. *Woodwind* (flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon) are blown. *Brass* (trumpet, horn, trombone, tuba) sound from the player's vibrating lips against a mouthpiece — cupped on the trumpet and trombone, funnel-shaped on the horn. *Percussion* (such as the timpani) are struck. Learn the four sound-makers and you can place an instrument you have never met, which is what the exam asks.

teach.smartTip: Four families, four ways of starting a sound: bowed or plucked, blown, buzzed through the lips, struck.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Pizzicato’ is Italian for ‘pinched’ — the player plucks the string with a fingertip instead of drawing the bow across it, giving a short, bright, detached note.

lessons.title: The clefs instruments read, and how to play

objectives: Instruments read the clef that fits their range — the viola reads the alto clef you just learned
Playing directions tell the player how to sound a note, not how fast to go
Arco and pizzicato are a pair, and so are con sordino and senza sordino

concept.title: Which clef, and how to play
concept.body:
Each instrument reads the clef that keeps its notes on the stave with the fewest ledger lines. The violin and flute read treble. The cello and double bass read bass. The viola reads the alto clef — which is exactly why that clef was worth learning, since the viola is the only common instrument that lives in it.

Composers also write directions telling the player how to sound a note. *Arco* means with the bow and *pizzicato* means plucked, so one cancels the other on a string part. *Con sordino* asks for the mute and *senza sordino* takes it off again. These say how to play, never how fast — a tempo word does that.

teach.smartTip: Arco cancels pizzicato and senza sordino cancels con sordino. Each direction has an undo.
teach.didYouKnow: 'Pizzicato' is Italian for 'pinched' — the player plucks the string with a fingertip instead of drawing the bow across it, giving a short, bright, detached note.

objectives: Recognise the Grade 4 Italian words for mood and attitude
A character word never changes the tempo
Con brio pairs 'with' to a noun, the same way con forza does

concept.title: The mood, named in Italian
concept.body: Grade 4 adds fifteen Italian words, and this is the half that names a mood. *Affettuoso* asks for tenderness, *amabile* for a pleasant, amiable manner, *appassionato* for passion. Against those sit the darker ones: *mesto* is sad and mournful, *misterioso* mysterious. Two are about attack rather than feeling: *deciso* is with determination and *con brio* with vigour — 'con' again followed by a noun, exactly as in con forza. *Ritmico* asks for the rhythm itself to be brought out. None of these touches the speed: allegro con brio is allegro, played with more edge.

teach.smartTip: If a word names a feeling, it is not the tempo. Find the tempo word separately.
teach.didYouKnow: Beethoven marked a movement con brio more often than almost any other composer. It is the difference between the right notes and the right performance, and the only part a metronome cannot help with.

lessons.title: Italian words for speed and time

objectives: Recognise the Grade 4 Italian words that set or change a speed
Stringendo drives forward; rubato bends the time without changing it
Alla breve sets the beat, not the speed

concept.title: Speed, and freedom with it
concept.body: The other half of the Grade 4 Italian is about time. *Larghetto* is rather slow — the *-etto* ending softens largo, so larghetto is less slow than largo, not more. *Comodo* (or *tempo comodo*) asks for a comfortable speed and *come prima* for the speed you had at first. *Stringendo* drives gradually forward. *Rubato* (or *tempo rubato*) is different in kind: it gives the player freedom with the time — literally 'stolen time', taken from one note and paid back to another. *Assai* means very and qualifies whatever it follows, so allegro assai is very fast. *Alla breve* is not a speed at all: it says the beat is a minim, two in a bar.

teach.smartTip: The -etto ending softens a word. Larghetto is less slow than largo.
teach.didYouKnow: Rubato means stolen. The old rule was that time borrowed from one note had to be repaid to another, so the bar still lasted exactly as long — the freedom was inside the bar, not on top of it.

objectives: Recognise the six French words the syllabus sets at this grade
Lent is slow, vite is quick, modéré is a moderate speed
Retenu holds the speed back

concept.title: Speed, in French
concept.body: From Grade 4 the paper can mark a piece in French, and six words are set. Four of them are speeds and read straight across: *lent* is slow, *modéré* a moderate speed, *vite* quick, and *animé* animated. *Retenu* pulls the speed back — the Italian equivalent is ritenuto, and the two even look alike. *Douce* is the odd one out, naming a manner rather than a speed: soft and sweet, the French for dolce. French marks are often written as a verb telling the player what to do, where the Italian names a state, which is why so many of them end in -é or -ant.

teach.smartTip: Each French word here has an Italian twin you already know. Retenu is ritenuto, douce is dolce, lent is lento.
teach.didYouKnow: Debussy and Ravel marked almost everything in French. Debussy went further and wrote whole performance sentences, not single words.

objectives: Read a passage drawn from the full Grade 4 vocabulary
Keep the reading order steady when there is more on the page
Answer questions that mix pitch, rhythm and metre

concept.title: More on the page, same method
concept.body: Grade 4 adds double dots, duplets, new metres and a wider set of keys, and a passage may use any of them. That makes the page busier rather than the questions harder, and the danger is reading in the wrong order: a learner who looks at the notes before the key signature will name the wrong pitch every time an accidental is implied. Keep the order. Clef, key signature, time signature, then notes. If a question asks about a bar, count the bars from the beginning rather than estimating — an examiner's answer is always exact, and an anacrusis is not counted as bar 1 — the first complete bar is.

teach.smartTip: Clef, key signature, time signature, then notes. The same order every time.
teach.didYouKnow: Examiners write the general-observation question last, after the rest of the paper is set, so that it uses only what the paper has already asked about.

objectives: Two notes are enharmonic when they sound the same pitch but are spelled with different letters
Every black key on the keyboard has two common names — one sharp, one flat
F♯ and G♭ are the same sound written two ways; so are C♯/D♭, D♯/E♭, G♯/A♭ and A♯/B♭

concept.title: The same pitch, two spellings
concept.body: On a keyboard the black key between F and G can be called F♯ (a semitone above F) or G♭ (a semitone below G). Same key, same sound — two names. Notes related this way are called enharmonic equivalents. Which spelling you use depends on what the note is doing: sharp keys lean on sharps and flat keys on flats, but the scale degree decides, which is why G♯ minor needs an F𝄪 rather than a G. The five black keys give the five common pairs: C♯/D♭, D♯/E♭, F♯/G♭, G♯/A♭ and A♯/B♭.

teach.smartTip: Keep the pitch, change the letter: an enharmonic equivalent always uses the neighbouring letter name — F♯ becomes G♭, never F♭.
teach.didYouKnow: On a piano the two spellings are the exact same key, but a string or voice can bend them apart a hair — many musicians play a G♭ a touch lower than an F♯, so the two names carry a subtly different feel.

lessons.title: Double sharps, double flats, and cancelling them

objectives: A double sharp (𝄪) raises a note by two semitones — a whole tone above the natural
A double flat (𝄫) lowers a note by two semitones — a whole tone below the natural
Name one by its letter plus “double sharp” or “double flat”: F𝄪 is “F double sharp”, not G
A natural cancels a double sharp or a double flat outright; a single sharp or flat cancels only half of it

concept.title: Raising and lowering by a whole tone
concept.body: You already met a double sharp inside a scale: the raised 7th of G♯ harmonic minor is F𝄪. A double sharp (written 𝄪, sometimes an ×) raises the letter by two semitones — F𝄪 sounds the same as G, but it is still spelled as an F because the key needs it that way. A double flat (written 𝄫) lowers by two semitones, so B𝄫 sounds like A. Keep the letter, name the accidental: F𝄪 is “F double sharp”, never “G”. A double accidental holds for the rest of the bar, exactly as a single one does, and a later sign on the same note replaces it rather than adding to it. A natural cancels the whole thing: after F double sharp, a natural gives plain F. A single sharp cancels only half of it, leaving F sharp. Older printing sometimes wrote a natural beside the new sign to make the change plain, but the sign alone is enough.

teach.smartTip: Keep the letter name and add the words: a double sharp on F is still an F — “F double sharp” — even though it sounds like G.
teach.didYouKnow: Double sharps appear whenever a key already full of sharps needs to raise a note further — like the F𝄪 leading note of G♯ minor. Composers keep the letter so the note still reads as the seventh degree of the scale, not a stray G.
